# AI models predict which UI components developers choose, up to 70% of the time


We showed 11 models 200 pairs of components from 21st and asked which one developers chose more often for their projects. Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.1 did best, and all of them prefer the plain option where developers go for gradients, glow and 3D.


Alex Smirnov


[@asmirnovxyz](https://x.com/asmirnovxyz)


How often each model picks the component developers prefer


200 pairs of 21st components


We showed 11 AI models 200 pairs of components from[21st](https://21st.dev/) and asked which one developers prefer. The best, Claude Opus 5.5


and Claude Fable 5.1


, got 70% right. A coin gets 50%.


## What we found


- **Models agree with developers on clear cases.** When both components are plain and developers strongly prefer one, nearly every model picks it too.
- **They don't share developers' taste for the bold.** Where developers go for gradients, glow or 3D, the models stay with the plain, safe option. A judge built on today's models would underrate the components developers actually want.
- **Developers forgive flaws that models punish.** Models point at bugs, cramped layouts and placeholders, yet developers sometimes pick that component anyway, likely because they will rework it in their own project.
- **More context doesn't fix it.** Live frames, video, source code and 40 solved examples barely moved the scores. The gap is in what the models prefer, not in what they see.
- **Closing it needs developers' own choices.** Prompting won't teach a model this taste. Training on what developers actually pick might, and 21st records such choices every day.


## The setup


On 21st a developer searches (for example "login") or opens a category page, sees a grid of component previews and copies the one they want. A copy means the component is going into their project.


The Login category page on 21st. Each card is a component preview, and a developer opens one and copies its code or a prompt for their AI agent.


For every search and category page we looked for two components that do the same job, were shown on that page over the same period, and where developers copied one far more often than the other. The one copied more is the one developers prefer.


Raw copy counts carry a lot of biases, from the position on the page to the component's age, its theme and how well known its author is. We corrected for each of them, as described inBiases in the developers' picks and how we removed them .


Each model sees the search text and the two previews with their names, and picks one. We call it directly through its API with the prompt below, with no agent harness and no tools.


Show the prompt


```text
On 21st.dev, a marketplace of ready-made React + Tailwind UI components, frontend developers look for a component for their own product (a landing page, a dashboard, an app) and copy the one they want into their project, usually as a prompt for their AI coding agent.


Developers searched for "{query}" and saw both components below on the same results page. Both do the same job. Over 45 days, one of them was copied at least 3 times more often than the other. We removed all outside factors (such as position on the page), so the difference comes from the components themselves.


Predict which one developers chose more often. Think as a developer who searched for "{query}" and is picking a component for a real product.


A: "{name A}"
[preview image A]
B: "{name B}"
[preview image B]


Reply with JSON only: {"answer": "A" or "B", "confidence": probability 0.5-1.0 that your answer is right, "why": "one sentence"}
```

## What we tried to close the gap


First we rewrote the prompt. Our first version was short and technical; the final one, shown in the setup, explains who copies components on 21st and why. It made no difference beyond noise.


Then we gave the models more to look at, with the same final prompt. The table shows how each change moved a model's score compared with the main run on one screenshot:


- **+ frames, video, description** : the screenshot developers see in the results plus four live frames from Chrome (on load, a moment later, on hover, scrolled), four frames of the hover video and the author's description.
- **+ source code** : all of that plus the component's full source code.
- **Screenshot + 40 examples** : before the question, 40 other pairs from our set with the component developers copied more. The pair being judged and any pair sharing a component with it are never among them.

None of the three changes moves the models beyond noise. Frames and video help the weaker models most, so a single screenshot sometimes hides something from them that the top models already see. Even 40 choices of this same audience don't teach the models its taste.


## Methodology


How we got the 200 pairs, in five steps:


1. **Copies.** Searches and category pages on 21st: which components were on the page, in which position, and which one the developer copied within 30 minutes. Many developers pay to copy, so a copy is a deliberate choice.
2. **Position correction.** The top result gets copied far more often whatever it looks like, so we compare each component with the copies its positions alone would give it.
3. **Pairs.** Two components shown on the same page. After the position correction, one was copied at least 3 times more often than the other. The winner has at least 5 copies, and the gap is too large to be chance.
4. **Filters.** We kept only pairs where nothing but the components themselves can explain the gap (table below). 200 pairs passed: 78 from 41 searches and 122 from 45 category pages.
5. **Models.** Each model got the prompt from the setup through its API (via OpenRouter, high reasoning effort where available, no tools), saw each pair in both orders, and scored half a point when its two answers disagreed. A model that always picks the same side scores exactly 50%.


How position correction works


Component A was shown 1,000 times, always first, where 1% of views end in a copy. Component B was shown 1,000 times, always tenth, where 0.25% of views do. From their positions alone we expect 10 copies for A and 2.5 for B. Both were copied 10 times. A got exactly what first place gives anyone, B got 4 times more than tenth place usually gets, so B is the one developers prefer.


In practice a component moves around, so we add up the copy rate of its position at every single showing over the whole period. Across 21st the first search result gets about 10 copies per 1,000 views, the tenth 2.2 and the twenty-fifth 1.0.


### Biases in the developers' picks and how we removed them


By "developers' pick" we mean the component of a pair that developers copied more. These picks are stable: split the users into two random halves and the same component wins in 98% of pairs in both, and paying subscribers alone agree with everyone in 95–97%. Still, some things other than the component itself can sway copies. Every pair passed these filters:


Filter Why


Both at least 30 days old Newer components win more often, just for being new


Paywall on under 5% of opens Behind a paywall, copies depend on the developer's plan, not on the component


Same job, both fit the search, not a fork Many pairs on one page do different jobs (in "dashboard", a sidebar against a chart)


Both light or both dark Dark or light depends on the developer's project, not on quality


Both previews show the component, each pair counted once, checked by eye Empty or mid-animation previews and repeats of the same two components were dropped


We did not filter on how well known the authors are: the winner's author is the more popular one in 98 of the 200 pairs, about half.


### Biases in comparing the models


A model can score well or badly for reasons that have nothing to do with taste: it may favour one side of the screen, recognise a component by name, or catch a cue in the pairs that gives the answer away. Here is what we checked and how we handled it:


Possible bias What we found and did


Order of A and B GPT models lean to the second option, so every pair is asked in both orders


Remembering components by name Given only the names and the search text, the models do no better than a coin, so they decide from the images


Famous authors Models don't score higher when the winner's author is in the top 20%


Position Models never see positions, and the position correction removes its effect


Shortcuts in the pairs, such as the winner always looking bigger The weak control gets 54%, no better than a coin


Examples leaking answers Examples in the prompt never include the pair being judged or any pair sharing a component with it


### Limits


- Only large gaps of 3 times or more, from frequent searches and category pages. Closer calls would be harder.
- This is the taste of developers picking ready-made components on 21st, mostly as prompts for their AI agent. It may not carry over to designers or end users.
